source.title: Steering grids for sparse-autoencoder features: when a top-context label names an activation regime rather than a causal axis

record.tranche_reason: Tests how feature interpretations change under different steering coefficients and interpretation/coherence measures, using SAE-feature steering rather than neuron analysis.
record.gate_note: The study tests SAE features in language models, not individual MLP neurons, and does not estimate how prevalent polysemanticity is. Its coefficient sweeps and alternative interpretation/coherence measures bear directly on V7. It does not test vision models, superposition as a cause, initialization or regularization, or activation-function comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study steers SAE decoder directions, not individual neurons. It measures how a feature's top-context label changes across steering coefficients, plus joint-suppression and random-direction damage. It reports no rate or degree of neuron polysemanticity and no test of superposition, capacity, architecture or measurement effects on neurons. SAEs are a tool built on the superposition and polysemanticity premise (Elhage et al. is cited only in related work). The results concern the authors' own SAE-steering protocol, so no version is tested. The reader's V7 link conflates SAE feature labels under steering with whether a neuron counts as polysemantic.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct for the coefficient-axis finding, but incomplete. The authors also conclude that three near-orthogonal features are jointly necessary for grounded composition, though individually substitutable. A matched-geometry random-direction control shows the damage depends on direction pattern, not magnitude, on all three models. The joint-condition effect holds at matched coefficient but only partly at matched geometry. Prevalence of incomplete labels is explicitly not estimated.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses SAE decoder-direction steering, coefficient sweeps, and output-based coherence and relabeling checks on language models; it does not reproduce neuron visualization or neuron-level tests from the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed interpretation varies with steering coefficient and with the coherence/labeling measure. On Qwen, the canonical loop-and-length detector reports 0% degeneration where lexical diversity is 0.46 of baseline and only 12 of 96 completions are lexically intact. The pre-registered screening rule also misses F-disc's known switch.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features labelled 'AI self-disclaimer' from their top contexts produce a different coherent surface form under steering at other coefficients: a contemplative voice on Qwen F-disc at c=+500 (coherent only in a minority of samples) and a collective we-voice on Gemma #3997 at c=-200 (clean by all reported signals). Blind relabelling of steered samples gives a cross-topic description.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-context labels of SAE features describe one activation or steering regime; steering across coefficients can reveal other output behaviours of the same direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Loop-and-length degeneration detectors report 0% in steering cells whose lexical diversity is about a third to a half of baseline. NLL under the unsteered model favours phrase recycling over genuine register change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard coherence detectors used in steering evaluations miss phrase-level degeneration.

record.problems: The paper reports no prevalence estimate; the Qwen contemplative form is fully coherent only in a minority of samples. Coherence thresholds are not calibrated against human judgments, and the study examines a limited set of SAE features and models rather than individual neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Joint-feature suppression, matched-geometry random-direction controls, and unrelated-feature-triple results in §§4.2–5 and Appendices I, K, L, M were not included because they concern grounded composition and steering damage, not the measurement-dependence version recorded here. Other dose-response and anchor results were not included where they do not bear directly on the coefficient/label/coherence measurement question.

untested.parts: Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer LMs and its variation by layer.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Effects of architecture, activation function or regularization on the polysemantic share.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons reduce to one shared feature.
Whether a neuron's polysemantic status depends on its activation range or on explanation scoring. The study examines SAE feature labels under steering, not neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 link is rejected. V7 concerns whether neurons count as polysemantic depending on activation range and explanation scoring. This paper concerns SAE-feature labels versus steering behaviour, and coherence detectors. Neither is a measure of neuron polysemanticity. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: MLP neurons, unrelated tokens or contexts, and layerwise prevalence in transformer language models.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization or training noise under sufficient capacity.
Activation-function, architecture or regularization comparisons, including SoLU or modern convnets.

Whether canonical polysemantic neurons generally resolve into shared features or related jobs, and whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare. The study examines SAE features, not neurons, and does not estimate prevalence.

The study tests coefficient range and interpretation/coherence scoring on selected SAE features; it does not establish how broadly these measurement effects generalize to neurons or other model families.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct, F-disc (#26221)
rows.operation_detail: Applied top-context labeling to baseline and steered sample sets using blinded Claude-Opus-4.7 labellers
rows.value: Both descriptions were topic-focused introspective-reflection descriptions; neither produced the original AI self-disclaimer label.
rows.uncertainty: Two independent labellers; verbatim agreement across two independent reruns is reported for the steered description, not this baseline condition.
rows.note: The paper states that baseline top-context samples did not expose the cross-topic framing property.
rows.check: Blind auto-labelling of an SAE feature from top contexts; not neuron polysemanticity.

conditions.value: 12 completions steered at c=+500 across six mixed intervention prompts

rows.baseline: Baseline descriptions were topic-focused introspective-reflection descriptions
rows.value: Both labellers described introspective philosophical contemplation framing applied indiscriminately to any topic.
rows.uncertainty: Verbatim agreement across two independent reruns at temperature 1.0
rows.note: The paper interprets the steered description as more informative about cross-topic application and causal role.
rows.check: Auto-label of steered samples for an SAE feature; bears on no version.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct, top 50 Class-1 SAE features
rows.operation_detail: Applied the pre-registered mode-switch screen across five coefficients and then inspected the flagged candidate
rows.measure: Candidates flagged by the pre-registered rule
rows.value: 1 of 50 candidates (2.0%; Wilson 95% CI [0.4, 10.5]%), rejected on inspection; an amended gate flagged 0 of 50.
rows.note: The screen did not flag F-disc's established switch because its rule requires a marker-rate fall; the authors say the screen's null reflects Qwen's diversity collapse at the relevant coefficients, not an estimate of prevalence.
rows.check: The pre-registered screen is the study's own method audit (detectability of mode switches), not a polysemanticity rate. It is closer to a selection or method-performance value than a result on the claim.
